pages.x: Mehmed was born in Edirne in 1432, son of Sultan Murad II. His father handed him the throne at 12, then took it back when the army rebelled and a crusade threatened. Mehmed never forgot it. He grew up speaking several languages and reading the lives of Alexander and Caesar.

A Hungarian engineer, Orban, cast him huge bronze cannons. The biggest fired stone balls of more than 500 kg and took 60 oxen to pull. For a thousand years the walls of Constantinople had never been broken.
In 1453 he besieged Constantinople. A great chain blocked the Golden Horn, its harbour, so he had about 70 ships hauled overland on greased logs, over a hill, and launched them behind the chain.

On 29 May 1453, after 53 days, his troops stormed the battered walls. The last Byzantine emperor, Constantine XI, died fighting. Mehmed rode to Hagia Sophia and made it a mosque. From then on he was called Fatih, "the Conqueror".

He made the city his capital, filled it with people of every faith, and named a Greek patriarch to lead its Christians. He built a great mosque and the Topkapi Palace, the home of sultans for 400 years.

Mehmed loved art and collected books in Greek, Latin and Arabic. In 1479 he invited the Venetian painter Gentile Bellini to Istanbul to paint him; the portrait of the sultan in a red cloak and white turban hangs in London.
Mehmed ended the thousand-year Byzantine Empire and made Istanbul the capital of an empire that lasted until 1922. To Turks he is Fatih, the Conqueror, one of their greatest heroes.
